word-professional-documents.title: Welcome to Word: professional documents, part of Microsoft Office.
word-professional-documents.idea: Almost every professional document starts as somebody else's draft: a proposal with a structure template, a report with sections to fill, a letter on company letterhead. The people who are trusted with these documents are not the fastest typists; they are the ones whose documents look consistent at page 40, whose contents page matches the headings, and whose tracked changes a reviewer can follow.
word-professional-documents.example: A twenty-two page report arrives for tidying. The headings were formatted by hand at six different sizes; the contents page was typed manually and no longer matches; page numbers start from the cover; three tables are unnumbered; and one table needs landscape orientation while everything else is portrait. The repair takes about two hours and follows the process exactly. First, all headings are re-tagged with real heading styles — the document immediately becomes navigable and the table of contents will be accurate. Second, the typed contents page is deleted and an automatic one is inserted, set to update on print. Third, a section break is added before the body so that the cover has no number and the body starts at page 1; the footer is set accordingly. Fourth, the landscape table gets its own section with the orientation changed, and its own header — Word's "link to previous" is switched off so the change does not affect the rest. Fifth, every table gets a caption, and the "see Table 3" references in the text become cross-references. The result: the document now updates itself, adding a section takes seconds and the numbering follows, and the same file can be re-templated for the next report by replacing the content and leaving the styles alone. That last point is the real prize — the template is reusable, and the next report takes forty minutes instead of two hours.
word-professional-documents.challenge: Produce a complete, delivered document — a report, proposal or manual of at least ten pages — using styles, an automatic table of contents, sections with correct page numbering, captioned and cross-referenced tables, a reviewed change log, and a checked PDF. Then save it as a template and use that template to produce a second, shorter document in under an hour, recording how long each took.

excel-spreadsheets-that-work.title: Welcome to Excel: spreadsheets that stay correct, part of Microsoft Office.
excel-spreadsheets-that-work.idea: Every office has one spreadsheet that everything depends on and nobody fully trusts. It was built by somebody who has left, its totals are copied from somewhere, and the number that goes to management is typed into a different file. Learning to build a workbook that a stranger can audit is a professional skill with immediate value — and half of it is refusing to type data into a decorative layout.
excel-spreadsheets-that-work.example: A school's fees spreadsheet has a layout with merged cells for each class, quarterly amounts in three columns, arrears calculated by hand in a colour-coded column, and a summary sheet where totals are typed from the class sheets. It takes a full day to update each term, and the totals can be wrong without anybody noticing. The rebuild starts with the data: one row per student per term, with columns Student ID, Name, Class, Term, Fee Due, Amount Paid, Payment Date, Method. Zero formatting, and every value a number or a real date. The calculations sheet adds a handful of formulas: Balance = Fee Due - Amount Paid, Status = IF(balance<=0,"Paid",IF(balance<fee*0.5,"Partial","Arrears")), and Days Overdue = IF(balance>0, TODAY()-DueDate, ""). Sums by class become SUMIFS. The report sheet uses a pivot table: class by term, with sum of Fee Due, sum of Amount Paid and count of students. Conditional formatting colours balances that are still positive. A dropdown list on Class and Method means the next person cannot misspell them. The measured change: a full-day update becomes about forty minutes, the class totals reconcile with the accounting system to the cedi, and the head teacher's weekly question — who has not paid — is answered by a filter rather than a search through four pages of colour coding.
excel-spreadsheets-that-work.challenge: Rebuild one real spreadsheet that your work depends on: a proper data sheet, a calculation sheet with documented formulas, a report built on a pivot table, validation on every input, conditional formatting for exceptions, a README sheet, and a reconciliation step that ties the totals to an independent source. Measure the time it takes to update the new version against the old, and report the reconciliation difference you found in the original.

powerpoint-presentations.title: Welcome to PowerPoint: presentations that work, part of Microsoft Office.
powerpoint-presentations.idea: The most common mistake in a business presentation is treating slides as a document: dense paragraphs, a table with thirty rows, and a presenter reading aloud. The audience reads ahead, stops listening, and remembers nothing. Slides are a visual aid for a spoken argument — and the discipline of building them that way makes the argument itself clearer.
powerpoint-presentations.example: A quarterly review deck arrives with 34 slides, each a paragraph of 8 pt text, three tables of numbers and a template of stock gradients. Nobody in last quarter's meeting could recall the conclusion. The rebuild starts from the claim: the quarter's performance against target, and the decision requested about the north region's stock levels. Everything that does not support that claim is cut — the 34 slides become 11, and two of the cut slides are moved to an appendix for questions. Each remaining slide gets a headline that states a conclusion rather than a topic: not "Northern region sales" but "Northern region is 18% below target because of stock-outs in two SKUs". The numbers become one chart per slide with a single highlighted series, and the tables move to the appendix. The gradient template is replaced with a master using the client's actual brand colours, and the type is set at 32 pt headlines, 20 pt body. The result in the meeting is measurable in behaviour rather than in aesthetics: the presentation takes nineteen minutes instead of forty, four of the six questions are about the decision rather than about what a number means, and the decision is taken in the meeting instead of being deferred for clarification. The slides did less, and achieved more.
powerpoint-presentations.challenge: Build and deliver one real presentation of ten to twelve slides to a live audience: a master with consistent type, claim headlines, at least two charts and one photograph, an appendix for detail, and a closing slide that asks for a specific decision. Record the questions you were asked, and write down which part of the argument the audience found least clear — then fix that slide and present it again to somebody who was not there.

collaboration-and-shared-files.title: Welcome to Collaboration: files, email and shared work, part of Microsoft Office.
collaboration-and-shared-files.idea: The cost of file chaos is invisible until it is enormous: a proposal sent with an outdated price, a report edited by two people in parallel, a term's marks recovered from a backup phone. The tools that prevent it — shared drives, co-authoring, version history — have been standard in Microsoft 365 for years and are still commonly unused, which is why they are a skill worth learning deliberately.
collaboration-and-shared-files.example: A three-person consultancy prepares proposals. The process was: one person drafts, emails the attachment; a second edits it and emails back proposal-v2.docx; the third plays with formatting and sends proposal-FINAL.docx to the client. One week, the client received a version with last quarter's prices, because the number had been changed in a copy that never merged. The new workflow uses the tools rather than willpower. A SharePoint library, Proposals/<Client>/, holds one file per proposal, named with the client and the date. Each proposal has an internal price sheet as a separate linked spreadsheet so the price lives in exactly one place. The three of them co-author in the browser; each edit is attributed, and a comment thread records why the price changed. A Team's channel gets the notification when a file is ready for review. When the price sheet was edited the following month, the change was visible in the version history with who changed it — and the proposal itself pulled the new figure automatically. And when somebody accidentally deleted a paragraph of the executive summary the day before sending, the version from two days earlier was one right-click away. The rules that made the difference take two sentences: one file, one place, one price; and the link goes to the client, not the file.
collaboration-and-shared-files.challenge: Establish a working file system for a real team or organisation: a folder structure with naming rules and permissions, a co-authored document with comments and version history in use, a client-facing share set to view-only with an expiry, and a backup routine that keeps an independent dated copy off the synchronised drive. Write one page of simple rules for the people who will use it, and test it by having somebody new find and edit a file using only the rules.
